speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head V of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: One value proposition that we have been very successful at is in the area of developing Singapore as a regional hub, such as in air and sea transportation, petrochemical, trading centre, finance and banking.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: While we know that many economies also have similar aspirations and many do want to model after the Singapore experience, with enough capital, there is no stopping these countries in the region from building and replicating physical hubs, such as ports, airports or other new specific theme hubs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: So, just competing on building more state-of-the-art physical infrastructure alone is not enough to maintain our superiority in the global connectivity race.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: We need to work on the soft attributes and continually develop the non-physical connectivity aspects in areas, such as the digital infrastructure, data risk capital, legal system and regulations, talent and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Minister how we could anchor ourselves as a key node in the global trade flows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: What are our plans to enhance both our physical and non-physical connectivity?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: The key words that I picked up are "scale up and growing our enterprises".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: We have a diverse enterprise landscape of about 200,000 companies, from micro-enterprises to large firms, each with varying level of value contribution and labour productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Hence, a one-size-fits-all approach will not be an optimal strategy and not an effective use of resource.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: In this deepened phase of transformation, what is needed to help promising companies are more customised approaches to support enterprise growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Can I ask the Minister how the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and the economic agencies intend to support and help the different sizes of companies to transform and to improve productivity?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Understandably, the tightening of foreign workers' quota will be painful to some companies which are unable to find local workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: There are many of the smaller companies who are still heavily dependent on foreign labour to sustain their businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: How can we help these businesses reduce their dependence on foreign labour?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: How could we help the enterprises to be more labour-efficient by adopting technology and digitalisation?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: How can we help companies to improve productivity and be in a position to hire more local workers and to support our Progressive Wage Model?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: By being the representative organisation with its outreach and network, TACs can be an influential multiplier and help bring more companies on board into sectoral transformational efforts, such as Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: In our Government Parliamentary Committee for Finance, Trade and Industry engagement with businesses as well as the TACs, the TAC leaders shared about the heavy workload and pressures they are under, subjected to, to participate in the ITM-related transformation efforts and work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: They feel a great sense of heavy responsibility on their shoulders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Some TACs said that they only have about five to six headcounts in their association, and their leaders are themselves facing severe business challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Can I also ask whether those TACs that are involved in the ITMs, are they adequately resourced and ready to support the next phase of a much deeper transformational effort?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: Well, it is their business call, and we have to respect that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: So, can I also ask the Minister what have we done to enthuse businesses with the external opportunities out there, the network and the trade partnership that we have established?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: How can we get the companies to see the better commercial returns by seeking growth, innovation and improving productivity?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah
text: What are the enablers that we need to further strengthen and create to enhance our overall value proposition?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The usual peak season at the end of 2018 did not happen for some of the sectors.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The services sector is maintaining its growth trend.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Manufacturing, being a pillar of our economy, over-reliance on this sector is a concern unless the manufacturing sector transforms itself to a higher value-add.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As many local businesses are concerned with 2019, they harbour some of the hopes and dreams to go overseas.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But what are the plans the Government has to implement a higher range of growth for the forecast, as well as strengthening the enterprises?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Though I believe there is some investment sense in not putting all our eggs in one basket in all sectors, we have to be selective with our limited resources.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the specific sectors that the Government may want to look at to help uplift the growth to the higher range of our forecast?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to any initiatives and support from the Government, it is imperative that Singapore's well-calibrated approach to regulation is maintained so that our businesses continue to stay competitive to tap on opportunities in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the initiatives that the Ministry has undertaken to prepare our businesses to better seize the opportunities presented by the impending ASEAN expansion?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Are the planned initiatives to help businesses explore the ASEAN region different from those of the BRI?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the ASEAN region has been growing in affluence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Governments have been more willing to invest in recent years, and many are eyeing the sectors in which Singapore is leading in the region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of our neighbours are also doing a good job catching up with us.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Batam, for example, has increased in investments to develop local shipping and manufacturing sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Malaysia, they have been building up their ports and getting into the oil tanking business in a big way.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the oil companies are also taking up the storage tanks to store their oil cargoes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Penang and Kuala Lumpur, besides Bangkok in Thailand, offer competitive prices for those seeking medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The strong Singapore dollar has also been a factor in encouraging medical tourism to other locations in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our strategic location has given us an edge in the region, but we must take more proactive measures to enhance our global connectivity and continue to position ourselves as a key node in the global flows, especially within the ASEAN region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will apply not only to physical connectivity like our airport and air routes but also non-physical modes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can MTI provide updates on the Ministry's efforts to enhance our modes of connectivity in the region?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore's economic transformation over the last few decades owes much to its position as a regional and global economic hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Indeed, Singapore's economic history is rooted in its beginnings as a thriving, open port.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As we stand at the dawn of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, how can we continue to build on our status as a world-class "hub", leveraging such technologies as self-learning machines, robots, autonomous vehicles and the Internet of Things?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These new technologies will generate huge waves of change, transforming the way we work, live, consume, trade and invest.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The emerging technologies will exert disruptive impact on jobs, firms and overall economies at an unprecedented speed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a small open economy, our response must be to embrace the technological advancements to come and to use them as new opportunities for ourselves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I believe Singapore is well-poised to deploy our strengths towards fulfilling this vision.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa said, other countries and regions are not standing still.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: According to innovation strategist Charlie Ang, countries and their companies can attain sustained economic supremacy if they possess leading edge, proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The infusion of superior AI technologies into national industries, exported products and digital platforms is likely to be the next source of national competitive advantage.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What can we learn from established centres, such as Silicon Valley, whilst carving out a unique proposition that distinguishes us, Singapore, from other emerging centres, such as the Greater Bay Area?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How much risk are we willing to tolerate in this journey towards rapid and breakthrough innovations?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What new social compact do we need to foster with our citizens as we venture boldly into unchartered waters fraught with risks and failures, but rich with untold rewards and returns?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, physical and non-physical connectivity has traditionally underpinned Singapore's success as a Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As ASEAN and the larger Asian region continues to grow, they are also becoming better connected to the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Across the world, technology is also changing the way people and business connect with one another, as well as shortening and shifting supply chains and value chains.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is essential for Singapore to constantly review the current and future plans for both our physical and non-physical connectivity, so that we can stay ahead of the game and tap on new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So many businesses, unfortunately, are unaware of what advantages these agreements bring to their businesses, especially those smaller local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: FTAs are an effective platform to encourage internationalisation of companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, it is unclear if any companies are tapping on it.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: FTAs should also enable the efficient flow of trade volumes through technology and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: There is also a need to review FTAs which may not be meeting the original objectives or did not impact the trade flows, the bilateral trades of the two countries or the region.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is also important to develop such relationships and build up new FTAs with emerging markets and countries.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: However, we should not jump ahead of the capacities of our local companies when building up or developing these FTAs because it may lead them to disappointment and, worse, great losses to the company.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: And what can be done to connect our local companies to these platforms that the FTAs can potentially help them?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: With the rollout of ITMs for 23 sectors, the focus has been on strengthening companies by transforming them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Transformation also meant changes in processes, business models and strategies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: This will certainly impact employees at all levels within the companies that are undergoing transformation or change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: There will be resistance to the change, and ITMs may not reach the level of success that would make a difference or what is expected.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I believe there are three aspects of transformation that will impact the workers directly.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: First, the job redesign, change in the process, change in the scope of the job.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Second, job shift, the job itself is no longer available and they have to change sectors.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Thirdly, job displacement, that is, when the job they had is absolutely obsolete and there is no way the workers can find any other jobs with the current skillset or even upgrading some of the skillsets to the next level.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Of course, we can say it is still a mindset shift and they are unwilling to change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But how can we help these workers, how can we help these employees, especially when those whose companies are undergoing transformation change to a great level?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we expressly identify job redesign for older workers as a key component of each ITM?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we set out among the suite of initiatives on improving productivity in any given industry, meaning, making job redesign for older workers part of the suite of initiatives for improving productivity in any given industry so that we may spur the collective thinking that can go into finding better solutions of job design for older workers and channel some of the industry's efforts in innovation in this direction?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, resources could be pooled by companies in the industry to develop best practices to modify tools and equipment for use off-the-shelf by older workers throughout the industry.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As businesses in our industries think about how to change, or even disrupt processes in the workplace in order to generate greater value, on the back of better used resources, could we make job redesign for older workers a required part of the syllabus?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We know productivity is one of the four pillars supporting the growth and competitiveness plans of an ITM.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we envision job redesign for older workers as a key component of the ITMs perhaps as a third horizontal, along with promoting infocomm technology (ICT) adoption and skills development?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It can help to support the industries and produce improvements across the economy in the face of an ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: In my capacity as the current President of the Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF), we work at different levels to encourage manufacturing businesses to explore the different industry roadmaps.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Can the Ministry share if it has plans for more impactful communications and assistance to reach a wider audience and, in so doing, lend a hand to the ground efforts of TACs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Land Transport Authority's figures at end-2018 show Singapore’s electric vehicle fleet to be small.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we not do more to promote adoption of electric and hybrid vehicles?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But other countries have introduced reduced parking, reduced road usage fees and other incentives which go further than what we currently offer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Raising the diesel tax will not help the environment unless there are attractive, cleaner options as my colleague Mr Dennis Tan argued in his Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, can we not accelerate developing a network of charging and/or battery swapping stations island-wide?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Following on from an earlier Parliamentary Question I filed, I would also urge the Government to reconsider setting a date far into the future for a total fossil fuel vehicle ban, as the United Kingdom (UK) and France have done.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A hard target in the long-term future would focus minds and get stakeholders to start planning for the inevitable, thus hastening its arrival.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can MTI share what are the new economic growth areas that it is currently pursuing?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With increased global demand for food, Singapore can capitalise on this trend even though we have limited production capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: After all, we have the knack of turning a disadvantage into a strategic strength.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can MTI update on the progress of such investments?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How does the Ministry plan to continue to develop Singapore into an urban, agricultural and ecocultural technology hub?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we better help Singaporeans who are interested in this sector?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I spent the first eight years of my working life in the Economic Development Board (EDB) and am aware that the manufacturing sector has always been a strong anchor of economy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy recommended building a globally competitive manufacturing sector, at around 20% of GDP, over the medium term.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This underscores the continued importance of manufacturing in our economy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We need to press on with this sector's transformation in order to seize opportunities offered by technology and changing market demands and value chains.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It increasingly encapsulates a value chain of activities, including services, such as design, research and development (R&D), logistics, marketing and after-sales services.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The closer nexus between manufacturing and services has encouraged manufacturers to incorporate services elements into their businesses to differentiate their products and enhance their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In MTI's Committee of Supply (COS) last year, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon spoke about how the global manufacturing landscape is evolving due to rapid technological developments, and quoted areas, such as robotics and industrial Internet-of-Things.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What are some of the promising growth areas which our manufacturing companies can tap on as a result?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Given the pace of change, what can our companies do to capitalise on these technological developments and stay ahead as we transit to Industry 4.0?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What is the Government doing to support the growth of our manufacturing sector?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I understand that MTI has put focus on this and extra emphasis to assist local companies in the past two years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While I support the ongoing efforts, it is equally important for us to recognise the need to continue developing organic companies and groom them into a full-fledged business or industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, encouraging the creation of many startups do not naturally translate into building an industry or development of large local enterprises.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While consolidation and acquisition of businesses are a normal process, what seems to be a trend in our successful local enterprises is the lack of perseverance in building businesses where there is product or service expertise coupled with intellectual property (IP) knowledge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Further, some of these successful local enterprises tend to cash out as soon as the opportunity arises instead of attempting to develop the business to greater heights.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This, in the long run, will impede our ability as an economy to have large local enterprises that can contribute meaningfully to our GDP or our workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: By not expanding the base business or retaining core expertise in Singapore, it may be difficult over time for us to attract the multinational corporations (MNCs) in continuing investments in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have two suggestions for MTI to consider supplementing what exists today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Grants that are also given need to be customised and assessed on specific grounds that may not exist in today’s business context or agency's definition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Have that flexibility to review, and the agency officers who review these grants must have some level of business experience or exposure that allows them to understand commercialisation and business cases so that they can better provide these approvals not on the basis of against a checklist.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: ESG is providing currently a suite of services that I must say the contact leads in overseas markets have proven to be useful for some of the companies venturing abroad.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will be a tremendous help for the startups or local large enterprises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Japanese companies often share certain types of information among themselves relating to overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Japanese business centres are also commonplace in Asia, providing cheap, good locations for firms just starting up in Asian countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Japanese and Korean conglomerates are also known to bring suppliers from their own countries when they go abroad.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Has competition among companies in the same industry been an impediment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This kind of tender surveillance is a very simple yet practical form of support that operationalises the idea of hunting in packs, since our Singapore companies would jointly share the cost for such tender surveillance customised to their needs.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, innovation and R&D are key enablers of success in Industrialisation 4.0.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: According to the National Research Foundation, Singapore has built a cluster of globally impactful universities and specialised research institutes staffed by cohorts of researchers doing cutting-edge research.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There are also numerous research collaborations with industry partners, though most are with large corporations.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We are only seeing R&D investments in startups bearing some fruit lately.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There appears to be an important gap in this whole plan.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The biggest potential here is the commercialisation of military technology, as has been shown by the US and Israel.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Israelis have become renowned worldwide in efficiently effecting technology transfers to commercialise military technologies for civilian applications to benefit their economy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Technology transfers have been moving one way, benefiting our defence sector.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) and the Defence Science Organisation (DSO) have been working with the private sector to tap into the new technologies of Industrialisation 4.0 to enhance defence capabilities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Economic defence is one of the six pillars of our Total Defence strategy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Our SMEs are an integral part in economic defence.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Integrating them into the research and innovation sector is a key thrust of the RIE2020 Plan.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The objective of strengthening our companies is to prepare them for the future and to compete effectively overseas.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: For several years, we have been asking them to transform to digitalise, to automate, but it is difficult for some of the companies, especially those in the services sector.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I have recently visited companies which deal in flower arrangements and packaging of flower gifts as well as small businesses that deal with preparing "chwee kueh" and other local food.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I wonder how they can digitise, and they were asking me, "Since you have been in business, how do we digitise some of these processes when we have a winning formula here using a lot of labour?" For some companies, they may not be able to transform and look beyond what they already have.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It is difficult for them to scale as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But we should continue to push companies to continue to develop some ideas on how to automate the processes and also to develop their IP.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: I see a few aspects as well as potential for the companies to develop.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: It may not necessarily be automation or digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Third, it is leadership and mainly the mindset change of the leader.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We have to be able to foster the partnerships between the big and the small companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But it is not just by size, although size does matter.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: What is more important is to match and complement the knowledge or skills of these companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The creativity and innovation of each company complement the resources and strengths of the other company, if we draw them together into a partnership, that will strengthen them as a company as a whole.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: In coming to the new year 2019, we are looking at the future, and there will be a fair bit of consolidation for some of the sectors, especially with the concern on DRC.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Everybody is thinking about what to do with their own companies and their own sectors.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, it is important for us to look at some of the consolidation possibilities and combining the companies together and making them partner together.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: There are ways for consumers when they purchase products to be able to buy beyond their means of their income or income stream.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: They go into a hire purchase or instalment payment scheme, and that creates some problems.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: We have tight regulations on financial institutions in their lending platforms and also non-bank lending platforms in regulating them, making sure that they do not go beyond their means to lend out to those that they cannot do the Know Your Customer survey or assess their credit readiness.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: But for retailers, many of them go into the credit scheme where the consumers could live beyond their means, will purchase it and pay based on instalments.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And this is despite CASE signing eight Voluntary Compliance Agreements with these beauty- and slimming-related businesses asking them not to breach the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act (CPFTA).

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For many of these consumer complaints, they relate largely to businesses taking advantage of a consumer by exerting undue pressure or undue influence on the consumer to ask them to sign a contract, or businesses taking advantage of a consumer when the supplier or the business knows or ought reasonably to know that this consumer is not in a position to protect his own interests.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, the consumer is usually placed in a vulnerable position in an enclosed space because they are undergoing treatment at the business outlet.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, imagine, you get a coupon telling you that you can go for free treatment or treatment at a very low price.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And once you go for the treatment, midway through the treatment, the person providing the treatment puts undue pressure, tremendous pressure on you for the next one to two hours, asking you to sign up for a treatment package, or to sign a credit card for such a package.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, if you put yourself in that position, the consumer is really a captive audience where he or she is constantly being persuaded "you need further treatment", "this treatment is good for you", "signing a package would be of better value for you." Now, all these methods, Sir, are technically breaches of CPFTA.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, from CASE's experience, when we take up an application for injunction, the Court will require a high threshold to be met before the Court will grant any injunction for breach of the CPFTA due to such unfair practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For a consumer who had been pressured to pay for a package, the last thing he or she would wish to do is to commence legal action or go to Court to recover such payments.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, in our view, it may be easier to avoid the need for unnecessary Court litigation by imposing a mandatory cooling-off period on such industries.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This would provide a consumer, who had been subject to an unfair sales pressure with the right to cancel a contract within a certain period of time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The consumer can then obtain a refund of monies paid within this specified period, without this consumer needing to prove an unfair practice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I was told by the Hong Kong Consumer Council that they, too, are looking into legislating for a cooling-off period for the beauty and fitness services industry.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Another area of concern for CASE is the increasing number of consumers who are purchasing from entities incorporated overseas or from entities that may not be regulated under a consumer-related legislation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: An example would be consumers who bought their holidays from Agoda.com, Booking.com, Priceline.com and sg.hotels.com.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: All these entities are not licensed under the Travel Agent's Act and some are not even incorporated in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, they may not be regulated under existing legislation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And this is because such a mechanism will allow consumers to readily lodge a charge-back in instances of business closure.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In Hong Kong, card-issuing banks are required to comply with a Code of Banking Practice which provides that credit card-issuing banks must provide for reasonable channels for consumers to submit claims and to make such pertinent information available to consumers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In addition, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has further required all card-issuing banks to upload to their official websites, information about the charge-back dispute resolution process as well as the charge-back dispute resolution form.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, this will basically mean that consumers who have paid for their purchases using their credit card will be able to cancel the contract, go back to the credit companies and seek refund.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This can be immensely helpful to the low-income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, it can also be damaging if interest rates are high and if the said person is not financially-savvy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Through interactions with my residents, I have been made aware of cases where some of them were baited by low upfront costs and misleading advertisements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This led to them running into arrears because they eventually find themselves unable to cope with the instalment plan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I even had one resident asking if he could use his Central Provident Fund (CPF) to service the hire purchase fees for some items purchased from a furniture store.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Marketing campaigns and advertisements are bold with their plans and claims these days.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is not uncommon to see advertisements boasting "$0 upfront" payments, especially for expensive gadgets like smart phones.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Some instalment plans offer vouchers and goods-in-kind, very attractive freebies, to entice customers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Some offer payment plans spread out over 24 to 48 months, so the monthly instalment cost seems low.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: When you do the mathematics, it is much more expensive than paying for the price in full.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Those who are less financially savvy are less likely to keep proper financial records.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They may overestimate their ability to pay off the instalment plans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Although credit sales advertisements are often accompanied by disclaimers about the conditions of each instalment plan, these are usually in small print.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Even if the consumer has seen it, psychologically, their mind has already committed to the self-perceived good deal.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Coupled this with a very persuasive salesperson when one shops in person, and that is a guaranteed transaction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Most people do not realise they have made a poor purchase decision until perhaps months later when they find themselves grappling with the payments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, does MTI have plans to regulate the types of marketing done by credit sales companies or even hire purchase ones to entice buyers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One episode on Talking Point last year showed how individuals who do not have credit cards are given credit from certain retailers to purchase goods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I find it worrying that some merchants would persuade customers into parting with their money with no care about whether they will have problems paying it off later.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One major furniture company even cited that no minimum income is required for its instalment plans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On the surface, it seems like they are doing a good deed to help those who are short on money to purchase the furniture and then pay later.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But what happens later if the customers cannot afford the instalments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Has any check been done to find out how many customers purchasing goods and services under credit sales plans had to forfeit their deposits?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What will MTI do to ensure that the businesses and financial institution companies do not over-extend credit to consumers without checking their credit worthiness?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While there was no interruption of electricity services, weeks elapsed before a new contract could be called for and awarded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What recourse do households have against such retailers that unilaterally abandon their contract or are not able to fulfil it?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would households also be barred by EMA from claiming for their expectation loss and what compensation would be available should the retail price of electricity be significantly higher at the point of termination, to the detriment of the consumer?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, over the years, our processes and regulations have provided a safe and predictable environment for our people and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: With the emergence of new technologies and business models, it is important to ensure that our rules keep pace.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: If we are not flexible in our approach, we could easily lose our competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: A regulatory environment that supports innovation and risk-taking is, therefore, vital for our future economy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, there will be tradeoffs involved and difficult decisions to make.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Different regulatory agencies have their reasons for imposing rules and regulations.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Our regulatory framework must, therefore, strike a good and fair balance, so that our businesses can be competitive and our economy can create more good jobs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I note that the Pro-Enterprise Panel has worked with public agencies and companies to address many of these regulatory concerns that businesses face.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: More broadly, will our regulatory agencies be able to keep pace with the changes and develop regulatory frameworks that are needed for the future economy?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, this Chamber enacts laws, creates regulations and enables Government agencies to formulate rules.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: By updating our laws, introducing new regulations, we keep our governing framework current, effective and relevant to the needs of the society.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While many new regulations are conceived for their specific purposes, there can also be unintended effects and heightened compliance costs to those the regulations seek to serve.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: According to the arguments of Brexiteers, EU regulations are estimated to cost Britain a total of $120 billion per year.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The common agricultural policy alone reportedly cost £10 billion and indirect costs and by inflating food prices.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Some other economists estimate that the current regulations cost the UK 6% of its GDP.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: One of them, Prof Patrick Minford, said, "If Britain seizes the freedom to move away from the EU regulations, the current 6% could be cut by a third, boosting GDP by 2%." Chairman, while we are not debating the merit of Brexit here, it suffices to recognise the duality of regulations.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: There are tradeoffs, using benefits on one hand, but also increase compliance costs on the other.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: High compliance costs are not just a result of the need to conform to new standards per se but also the outcome of multiple inspection stations, longer inspection time, uncertainties in the final outcome of the test.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: New regulations added to existing ones can also lead to confusion.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They can be onerous and costly for businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Already, some businesses here have found it hard to navigate in an ever increasingly regulated environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How could our business associations and SMEs provide their feedback and suggestions to the Government on a regular basis with a view to improving regulations for certain industry sectors or for business in general?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their comments, questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we manage our near-term challenges, we must also keep a close watch on the longer-term trends that will impact our economic competitiveness and continued success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our near-term challenges include the uncertainties of US-China trade relations, the slowing Chinese economy, Brexit and various regional elections.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our medium-term and more significant challenges include shifts in global trade patterns, production chains and value chains brought about by technological shifts and geopolitics.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our future attractiveness as a choice business location will be shaped by the outcomes from ongoing discussions at international fora on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting and taxation principles for the new digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Despite the uncertain global context, there are reasons for us to be optimistic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we get our fundamentals right, we can further distinguish ourselves and attract global investors to come here and create better jobs for fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our fundamentals must include: first, effective governance founded upon long-term political stability, long-term planning, and a strong tripartite relationship that enables us to overcome challenges together.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must overcome the constraints of our geographical size by leveraging the digital economy and our connectivity, and embracing talent, technology and ideas from the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, a competitive advantage in innovation, creativity and standards, but not price.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must create a virtuous cycle where research and innovation translate into commercial opportunities and gain, which then enables further innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This must be supported by a progressive business environment with agile regulations and a strong IP protection regime.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our workforce must have knowledge of the region to value-add when others use Singapore as a platform.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As Mr Teo Ser Luck observed, our overall pace of growth is expected to moderate in 2019, and this will be uneven across sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While outward-oriented sectors are generally expected to see a moderation in growth this year due to the weaker external outlook, there remain some bright spots.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These include the information and communications sector, and the medical technology and aerospace segments within the manufacturing sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Such sectors are expected to do well, in part because they can leverage our extensive connectivity, and are also knowledge-intensive sectors that capitalise on our strengths in areas like high-quality standards and a robust IP regime.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In general, domestically-oriented sectors will need to push ahead with transformation efforts to improve their value-add and raise productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Performance varies across firms within each of these sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have seen good efforts by some firms, and will need to sustain the momentum and impetus for restructuring to uplift more firms within these sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how we can prepare Singapore for the next stage of growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To this end, we have a four-prong strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As a small economy, the world must be our hinterland.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must ensure global opportunities remain open to our businesses and people.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This means deepening and diversifying our linkages to overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will upgrade our trade agreements to secure deeper market access and updated rules that cater to new business models and regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: During our ASEAN Chairmanship in 2018, we completed several initiatives to boost ASEAN's attractiveness as a business and investment destination.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Five ASEAN countries are exchanging trade documents electronically, with the remaining countries coming on board this year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The ASEAN-wide Self Certification Scheme will save time and costs for our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, we must expand our network of FTAs to give our companies privileged access to more markets vis-a-vis our competitors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This ensures the diversification of our markets and supply chains, to not overly rely on any one particular market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Last year, we saw the entry into force of the historic Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This establishes our first FTA with Canada and Mexico.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This brings us one step closer to an FTA with our third largest goods trading partner and largest services trading partner.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We continue to make progress on the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) under Thailand's chairmanship in 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also broadening our reach by looking into FTAs with the Eurasian Economic Union, the Pacific Alliance, and the Southern Common Market in South America (MERCOSUR).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the longer term, we must increasingly take up opportunities in emerging markets by familiarising ourselves with the culture, regulations and business networks in regions that are newer to us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck asked about quantifiable indicators of how our companies have benefited from FTAs, and what can be done to increase their utilisation of FTAs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One of the key benefits for our companies from FTAs is tariff savings, which measure the dollar savings from our FTAs' lower tariffs for Singapore-originating goods.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These include broad-based FTA outreach sessions, assistance requested via the Enterprise Infoline and our SME centres, and customised one-to-one advisories for companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to work with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) and the TACs to help our companies utilise our wide network of FTAs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our trade agreements complement efforts by Singapore and like-minded countries to evolve international rules and uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system embodied in the World Trade Organization (WTO).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A major international effort is now underway to ensure that WTO remains relevant to the modern economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore is actively contributing as a co-convenor of the e-commerce Joint Statement Initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Initiative comprises 76 WTO members that have committed to negotiations to develop multilateral rules aimed at helping companies navigate the complex e-commerce landscape by reducing cross-border hurdles and giving greater certainty on regulatory rules.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We welcome further collaboration with like-minded countries to push the envelope on digital trade issues to build an open, inclusive, connected and predictable regulatory environment for businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we can build on our global air and sea hub status to create a unique value proposition that distinguishes us from others.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I agree with the comments that we need to go beyond hardware to include the wrap-around software to distinguish ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To bolster our hub status, we need to continue to deepen our physical connectivity while building "modern", non-physical modes of connectivity to be a key node in global flows.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) will share more on our efforts to strengthen our physical connectivity while the Ministry of Communications and Information will share more on our efforts to bolster our digital connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Douglas Foo also asked how the Government is helping our companies seize opportunities in ASEAN, as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) enhances integration and infrastructural links in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The China-Singapore Connectivity Initiative – New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor will facilitate trade flows between Southeast Asia and Western China through Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This includes our connectivity in terms of data exchange and customs facilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: ASEAN, with its rising middle class and rapid urbanisation, presents huge opportunities for Singapore companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To assist Singapore companies in their initial entry into overseas markets, we have also set up a Plug and Play Network which comprises 16 partners across nine markets globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This includes six ASEAN markets, and we will be expanding to Myanmar this year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In 2018, we launched Infrastructure Asia to facilitate investments and financing to support the infrastructure needs of the region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: By bringing together local and international firms across the value chain to develop, finance and execute projects, this enables infrastructure players to tap on opportunities in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are able to do all these because of our superior brand in terms of trust, the rule of law and our financial system.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As the economic landscape transforms, non-physical modes of connectivity will play an increasingly important role.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, data connectivity through the exchange of digitalised trade documents.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Networked Trade Platform can help businesses save time and cost by decreasing the need for paper exchanges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, we need to promote the flow of ideas and talent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Companies invest in Singapore because we have access to talent, both local and global.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For Singapore to thrive, we will continue to develop our local talent, and welcome global talent, especially those with high-end digital and engineering skills, to complement our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked MTI to share more about the Global Ready Talent Programme (GRTP) and the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, more than 50% of Singapore enterprises find it difficult to internationalise because they lack the right talent for their overseas operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To address this, we need to build a pipeline of local talent with the requisite in-market knowledge to identify growth opportunities and navigate challenges in overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will focus on markets in Southeast Asia, China and India.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: ESG will work with TACs and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to facilitate internship placements between companies and students.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also continue to promote the exchange of ideas and talent with innovation hubs around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Last year, on top of launching GIA in Bangkok, we also accelerated expansion plans, establishing GIA activities in France, Japan and Germany.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to expand the GIA network in 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our industry transformation efforts are off to a good start, with productivity growing faster in the last three years as compared to the first half of the decade.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate on how we will continue to transform our industries of today, while investing in new growth areas for tomorrow in order to benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Over the next three years, as the overall Services Dependency Ratio Ceiling (DRC) and its S Pass Sub-DRC are progressively lowered, we will walk alongside, and support, our businesses for the transformation journey ahead, through the following enhancements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will help more SMEs undertake deeper and more ambitious transformation as part of our economic restructuring.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will help the smaller companies adopt pre-scoped equipment and solutions to achieve the initial productivity boost.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa will be pleased to note that the enhancements will benefit our workers, too.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will streamline our efforts and resources with the Labour Movement so that we can collectively reach more businesses and their workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will do this by merging the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Inclusive Growth Programme (IGP) into the EDG from FY2020 and stipulating local employment outcomes that we expect grant recipients to fulfil as part of such support, so every project can expect to have local employment outcomes as part of their key performance indicator.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On top of this, we will work with SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) to support successful PSG applicants in their efforts to train their workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For us, business transformation must come together with skills uplifting for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The two are mutually related and cannot, and should not, be separated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: My colleagues Senior Ministers of State Koh Poh Koon and Chee Hong Tat will elaborate on these measures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister Josephine Teo will also share at the Ministry of Manpower's COS debate about how enterprises across all sectors can continue to tap on the Lean Enterprise Development (LED) scheme for transitional manpower support, where needed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond industry-wide efforts, transformation begins with each and every enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To tackle the challenges ahead and turn them into opportunities, we will need to level up, scale up and team up our enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For enterprises that have a proven track record of growth, strong leadership and growth ambition, the new Scale-up SG programme can support them in the next leap of growth to become our future industry leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: ESG will work closely with these enterprises and expert partners to identify priority growth themes, provide customised guidance on the execution of their business plans, and provide access to valuable networks and connections.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will elaborate on Scale-up SG and our enterprise-centric approach to move away from grants to support enterprises in levelling up and teaming up to build real capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we agree fully with the comment that we need a customised approach and it will not be a one-size-fits-all approach for all our 200,000 enterprises that are of varying sizes with differing needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our final strategy is to ensure that we have an ecosystem that empowers businesses and consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Tan Wu Meng will speak about the enablers we are developing to support a well-functioning market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This includes creating a pro-enterprise regulatory environment, promoting competition, and protecting consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, I have outlined the measures in place to ensure that the Singapore economy is prepared for its next phase of growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: By developing markets, industries, enterprises and enablers, we can be confident of overcoming our limitations of size and punching above our weight.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will include making sure that our workers keep pace with the skills upgrading necessary for them to get better jobs with better pay.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Economic growth cannot be an end in itself.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is the means by which we generate good jobs and better wages for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is the strong foundation upon which we build our social progress and mobility.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Amidst global uncertainty, Singapore can once again distinguish ourselves by transforming ourselves to take advantage of new technologies and new markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Together, we can create a better future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore is a small and open economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To remain globally competitive, we need to transform our industries and develop new areas for growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singaporeans must benefit from the new opportunities that industry transformation brings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have seen friction and instability arise in other parts of the world when workers feel they are left behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We should learn from these developments and ensure that both our companies and our workers share the gains from transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Chairman, allow me to provide an update on our ongoing efforts to transform our industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the next phase, we will be developing synergies across sectors to build and deepen linkages between the complementary industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In this way, industry stakeholders along different parts of the value chain can come together to innovate and ride on market opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This includes strengthening our partnerships with the TACs, which Mr Douglas Foo spoke about, through the LEAD programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: My colleague Senior Parliamentary Secretary Tan Wu Meng will elaborate further in his part of the speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our transformation efforts have begun to bear fruit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, in line with efforts to strengthen supply chain and logistics capabilities in the Trade and Connectivity Cluster, the Centre of Innovation for Supply Chain Management in Republic Polytechnic has rolled out several initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One of which, the GoLEAN Improvement Programme, helps companies systematically optimise their processes through building a culture of continuous improvement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has also resulted in shorter lead time to deliver orders, better customer service, and lower processing cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: More importantly, by working closely with the unions, SATS-BRF Food was able to sustain these productivity improvements and thereby improve welfare for its workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They are now able to start their shifts at more convenient times and some have seen wage increases made possible by job redesign.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Another promising growth area undergoing rapid transformation is Advanced Manufacturing, which Mr Baey Yam Keng spoke about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are building new niches in areas, such as additive manufacturing and advanced materials, by deepening the capabilities of our companies and workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Singapore Smart Industry Readiness Index was developed by EDB and leading global technical service provider TUV SUD and launched in November 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is a diagnostic tool for companies to evaluate their readiness for Industry 4.0.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The unions have also been important partners in building our capabilities in advanced manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, NTUC, the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i), EDB and the Metal Industries Workers' Union have recently engaged 16 major players in the manufacturing sector, such as Epson, Seiko and Natsteel, on the adoption of the Index and the training that is available for their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Such tripartite partnerships are very important in ensuring that as companies upgrade to new technologies, our workers also upskill into higher value-added jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, we are also developing next-generation estates, such as the Jurong Innovation District (JID), which will catalyse the Advanced Manufacturing cluster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: JID will feature innovative infrastructure, such as an underground District Logistics Network, that will free up surface land and provide seamless integration with JID buildings to transform the way we deliver goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond physical infrastructure, we are creating platforms for local and global talent to come together to exchange ideas and to collaborate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Last October, we hosted the inaugural Industrial Transformation ASIA PACIFIC (ITAP), an offshoot of the Hannover Messe, the largest Industry 4.0 event globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We look forward to hosting ITAP again this year to profile Singapore as the regional hub for Advanced Manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The growth of the advanced manufacturing sector will have spillover effects for emerging adjacent industries, such as electric vehicles (EVs), which Mr Leon Perera spoke about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In Singapore, players like Grab and ComfortDelgro have also been adding EVs and hybrids to their fleets, in line with the Government's push to encourage more carbon-efficient vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singapore's strong manufacturing and electronics sectors will allow us to plug into the global supply chain to meet the increasing demand for EV parts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We can also build our expertise in other nascent areas, such as self-driving software development and automotive cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Questions on plans for charging infrastructure and the use of EVs, unfortunately, fall under MOT, so I hope the Member perhaps will raise these questions at their COS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, in addition to transforming existing industries, we will also develop a new sector that offers exciting job opportunities – agri-technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The food and agri-tech sector is a $5 trillion global industry that is growing rapidly, fuelled by new innovations in processes and products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our good innovation climate, strong talent base, reputation for food safety and strategic location position us very well to capture a slice of this industry, particularly here in Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked how we are doing to develop this industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our vision is for Singapore to be a leading urban agriculture and aquaculture technology hub with a food production model that can be exported to the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To realise this vision, I am currently leading a multi-agency team looking at how we can better support the agri-tech industry in the areas of industry and enterprise development, R&D, manpower and regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This Steering Committee will work closely with industry players and associations, such as the Singapore Agro-Food Enterprises Federation, to take on board industry feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As we grow this nascent sector, we will encounter new challenges that will require us to explore regulatory flexibility and innovative ways of doing things.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, under the Singapore Civil Defence Force's (SCDF's) fire code, farms are regulated in much the same way as factories because production activities, such as packaging, are allowed onsite.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, some of the fire code requirements may not be applicable for farming activities and may constrain a farm’s operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Local egg farm, Chew's Agriculture, faced such difficulties when seeking fire safety approvals for its new farm at Neo Tiew Road.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are also helping more of our agri-companies expand into foreign markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, Sustenir, a local startup which specialises in the production of non-native plants, recently launched the first strawberries grown here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It has worked with ESG to develop regional marketing capabilities and is expanding its operations to Hong Kong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond the hardware and infrastructure, a talent pipeline is crucial to succeed in this endeavour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: More Singaporeans, especially younger ones, are showing interest in high-tech urban farming.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are now seeing an emerging new generation of young technopreneur farmers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We agree with Mr Desmond Choo that interested Singaporeans must be equipped with the specialised and relevant skills to benefit from opportunities in agri-tech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our IHLs have been instrumental in driving these efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, Republic Polytechnic has launched a Diploma in Urban Agricultural Technology early this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As the sector develops, we expect more of such course offerings from our other IHLs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will pool together resources, IP, infrastructure and expertise from Government agencies, IHLs and Research Institutes, which companies and practitioners can tap on to deepen their capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These developments will support our agri-tech sector in becoming an export industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our position as an agri-tech hub will strengthen Singapore’s economy, create good jobs for Singaporeans and buttress Singapore's food security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Food is important to us not only as an industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But it is something that is close to every Singaporean’s heart.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even in our communities, interest in urban farming is growing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For instance, the Citiponics Farm @ Ang Mo Kio is a pilot project located in my own constituency in Yio Chu Kang, on the rooftop of a multi-storey Housing and Development Board (HDB) carpark at Level 6, Block 700, Ang Mo Kio Avenue 6.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is the first time we are piloting commercial urban farming on an HDB multi-storey carpark, and it is another example of how our Government agencies like AVA and HDB have exercised regulatory flexibility to support the agri-tech industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This farm will hire local residents, including the elderly, and provide them with on-the-job training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: My elderly residents from the Asian Women’s Welfare Association (AWWA) Senior Community Home are very excited to have the chance to bond with one another by exercising their green fingers and, at the same time, earn for themselves a source of income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC FairPrice at the nearby Ang Mo Kio Hub will be one of the first buyers of the farm’s produce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Planting had started last month in February 2019, with the first harvest expected in April 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, residents can soon look forward to fresh vegetables that are produced by the community, in the community and for the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, industry transformation must not be an end in itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is a means to expand human capabilities and open up new opportunities for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In my time with the Labour Movement and in MTI working with companies and workers, I observed that some companies have yet to translate increased productivity into tangible benefits for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
